Ce n’est pas qu’à Montréal que le jazz s: It’s not just in Montréal that jazz seems to be popular with Gen Z and the millennials who came before them.

Dans un bar du boulevard Saint-Laurent,: In a bar on Saint-Laurent Boulevard, the atmosphere is electric. A fervent crowd comes alive on the dance floor while others listen attentively, drinks in hand. The night is young, and so is the crowd warming up the room. Valérie Lacombe and Sam Kirmayer, both jazz musicians, describe the scene as they experienced it last fall while they were playing.
« Le bar était plein de jeunes, début vi: “The bar was full of young people, in their early twenties, who were really into it,” says the drummer. “For years, every time we played at one of the city’s jazz clubs, the audience was made up of white people in their 60s. And for some reason, when the bars reopened, there was a bunch of different people.
C’est un nouveau public qui sort, et qui: It’s a new audience that’s coming out, one that wasn’t there before. It’s different, like something is happening,” adds her partner, who is a guitarist and teacher.
Sam Kirmayer, guitariste et Valérie Laco: Sam Kirmayer, guitarist, and Valérie Lacombe, drummer, during a sound check. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Ce n’est pas qu’à Montréal que le jazz s: It’s not just in Montréal that jazz seems to be popular with Gen Z and the millennials who came before them. According to The Guardian, nearly 40% of jazz listeners on Spotify are under 30, a share that grows every year – and streams of jazz playlists are rising, as is their popularity. The Japanese fashion giant Uniqlo put out a collection of T-shirts inspired by 1950s album covers from the famed Blue Note label. And that’s not to mention the pop and hip-hop artists who team up with jazz musicians or who, influenced by the genre, have made musical shifts in recent years.
Ce regain d’intérêt, Valérie Lacombe l’a: Valérie Lacombe has noticed this renewed interest. “I think it has to do with the music itself, and with what we’re going through right now,” she says of the past few years, marked by COVID-19 and social tensions. “Wynton Marsalis said that jazz is a celebration of life, of its good times and its bad.
C’est tellement communautaire comme musi: It’s such a communal music. It does a lot of people good because what we’re living through right now is so hard,” she says. If young people are showing up, perhaps it’s because jazz has a cathartic dimension. “They also want to have an experience,” Sam Kirmayer points out. “Jazz is music that’s played live. Even if you listen to a band play the same tune twice, it’s never the same,” explains the guitarist, who adds that this music, more than others, is lived in the present moment and rests on spontaneity and expression. “Maybe that’s something people sense,” he says.
Les deux musiciens s’intéressent égaleme: Both musicians are also deeply interested in the history of jazz and the culture that gave birth to it.
« Les générations plus jeunes sont plus: “Younger generations are more outspoken and activist, and that’s part of jazz history too,” adds Valérie. “One of the effects of the Black Lives Matter movement was to spark interest in Black culture, and jazz is part of that,” Sam argues for his part. Both play a style of jazz called “straight-ahead,” a term for a way of playing that stays very close to the jazz tradition and is associated with Black American culture. The style, which some label “purist,” is rarely taught in schools and, according to the musicians, is neglected in the jazz world.
Et ils trouvent que c’est dommage. « À M: And they think that’s a shame. “In Montréal, there are different scenes, and many people write more contemporary-style compositions. Yet straight-ahead changed my life, and Sam’s too!” Valérie exclaims. “It’s the kind of music we want to share.”

La réputation de ville de jazz festive p: Montréal’s reputation as a festive jazz city precedes it. That reputation is reinforced by the Montréal International Jazz Festival, the largest in the world. The city also owes its fame to the Roaring Twenties. When Prohibition came into force, Montréal quickly became the go-to destination for a good time. From the 1920s on, the city was a must-stop for jazz musicians, and big names came to perform in local clubs.
Le quartier qui porte aujourd’hui le nom: The neighbourhood now known as Petite-Bourgogne is the stronghold of jazz in Montréal, as the murals honouring Oscar Peterson, Daisy Peterson Sweeney and Oliver Jones, which light up the walls of the area, remind us. Apart from these images, little remains today of that era and of the community that lived there. The place has had several names. For the Black population living in the multiethnic neighbourhood, it was the “West End.” Many residents worked for the railway companies, whose premises bordered the neighbourhood – one of the few employers open to Black people in the climate of racism that prevailed at the time. A community and businesses grew up around them, notably jazz clubs, whose influence became particularly great.
« Les clubs faisaient partie d’un circui: “The clubs were part of a circuit. The big names in jazz, like Miles Davis, were in town all the time,” says Sam Kirmayer. “Because they came, people built relationships, and the musicians got to play with them and learn from them. We were part of a culture.” The late 1960s were marked by an “urban renewal” project in the neighbourhood, undertaken by the City of Montréal under Mayor Jean Drapeau. That was when the area was renamed Petite-Bourgogne. From 1967 to 1973, the construction of the Ville-Marie Expressway, which cuts through the middle of the neighbourhood, led to mass expropriations that affected many middle-class Black families. The expropriations continued as much of the rest of the neighbourhood was demolished to make way for social housing, so much so that today it makes up the majority of housing in the area. From 1966 to 1973, the neighbourhood’s population fell from 14,710 residents to barely 7,000.
Les citoyens se déplacent vers d’autres: Residents moved to other neighbourhoods, and Black businesses and institutions suffered, as did the culture and the music. Nearby, Saint-Henri, which bordered Petite-Bourgogne at a time when the boundaries were blurrier, is where Oscar Peterson was born in 1925. He would go on to pay tribute to the neighbourhood with his piece Place St. Henri, from the Canadiana Suite, of which he said: “It’s meant to represent the little French neighbourhood of Montréal where I was born: Saint-Henri.”
Partout, Oscar Peterson est considéré co: Everywhere, Oscar Peterson is regarded as one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. “Oscar Peterson, you go anywhere in the world, and you know he’s one of the most famous Montrealers of all time,” says Sam Kirmayer. “Why isn’t Quebec jazz centred on Oscar Peterson?” adds Valérie Lacombe.
Elle offre une réponse. « C’est un anglo: She offers an answer. “He’s a Black anglophone, and many people feel he doesn’t represent Quebec,” she believes. “In the minds of white francophone Quebecers, you can’t associate him, or Oliver Jones, with Quebecers. They don’t consider it part of Quebec culture. If we start talking about the legacy of the Black community in Petite-Bourgogne, maybe we have to admit that Jean Drapeau’s project may have been to clean house and destroy an entire community.”
« Maintenant, il y a cette idée de jazz: “Now there’s this idea of Quebec jazz, our jazz – they’re trying to use jazz from a nationalist perspective in Quebec. But it was first and foremost the art of Black, anglophone people from a community that lived along the railway lines on the East Coast,” says Sam.
La murale « Hommage à Oliver Jones », à: The mural “Hommage à Oliver Jones” in Petite-Bourgogne.
‍<strong>« </strong>Il y a beaucoup de g: “ There are many people from Black communities who are at the origin of different styles of music,” notes Vladimir Delva, a hip-hop historian. “And at the beginning, a lot of music developed in the community, whether jazz or hip-hop,” he says, going on to describe a form of appropriation and co-opting that erases the Black contribution. “Jazz is something very cultural and local,” says Rito Joseph, an entrepreneur and educator. Through Expériences du Montréal Noir, Mr. Joseph offers educational walking tours on the history of Black people in the city, particularly in Petite-Bourgogne.
Il fait écho aux propos de Sam Kirmayer: He echoes what Sam Kirmayer and Valérie Lacombe have said. “ Beyond the music, there was a culture, in which many layers of society were involved. An entire part of society has been forgotten and pushed aside,” he says. With Black History Month having just ended, it was a chance to talk about it. “I think Montréal doesn’t care much about the history of Black Montrealers, except in February. To leave out Black history is to leave out history in general,” says Mr. Joseph. “We forget that when we talk about history, we’re also talking about local history. It’s a serious omission, because it prevents many things: a form of social cohesion, a sense of belonging, a sense of roots.”
« Je trouve que Montréal “tokénize” le j: “I feel that Montréal ‘tokenizes’ jazz. Is it a cultural identity? Are people interested in this part of the culture to forge an identity for themselves?” asks Mr. Joseph. He wants the role of the music’s pioneers, who are often overshadowed, to be recognized. He names the late Doudou Boicel, founder of the city’s first jazz festival, and Rufus Rockhead, a producer of shows featuring only Black performers. There is also the renowned bassist Charlie Biddles, a major figure and ardent champion of the Montréal jazz scene, who lived in Montréal from the age of 22, from 1948 until his death in 2003.
« Les instances du gouvernement doivent: “Government bodies need to understand that without these people, an entire chapter of Montréal’s history would be missing,” says Rito Joseph.
« Il faut que la jeunesse qui arrive sac: “The youth coming up need to know who these people are. When we talk about jazz, we talk a lot about the past, very rarely about the future, the present,” he adds, calling for more support and a better showcase for today’s talent.
<strong>Choisir la musique, et sa ville<: Choosing the music, and choosing your city
Montréal, c’est également la ville où Mo: Montréal is also the city where jazz musician Modibo Keïta grew up, and where he chose to build his career. Pandemic or not, work takes him all over the world, but what matters most to him is the success he has here. “In general, our industry is starting to understand that music needs to evolve in the interest of everyone.
Ça fait des projets intéressants, et des: It makes for interesting projects and interesting collaborations,” he observes.
Le musicien Modibo Keita dans son studio: Musician Modibo Keita in his studio.
En plus de ses talents de tromboniste, i: In addition to his talents as a trombonist, he is also a producer. The Shed, the concert he is currently working on, should have been presented in 2020; it will take place two years later, on April 1 and 2. All tickets have been sold for an evening of improvised jazz that will bring local and New York musicians together on stage. “The pandemic gives more value to live concerts,” believes Modibo, who won’t be on stage this time.
Ce sont 300 billets qui ont été vendus à: Some 300 tickets were sold in advance, and the event is so popular that a second date was added – and those tickets flew off the shelves too. “In a city like Montréal, where the practice of [jazz] is marginalized, where the art I make isn’t mainstream at all, it’s something I’m proud of,” he acknowledges. A professional musician for 15 years, Modibo describes jazz, his jazz, as “instrumental music that comes out of the African American tradition, or that considers the African American tradition a central point of the music being played.” Definitions and music evolve, that’s how he sees it. “For me, this is how I play, it’s what I learned and what my mentors do.” In Montréal, it’s a style you rarely hear.
« Il y a peu d’intérêt à créer un lien a: “There’s little interest in building a connection to this tradition because the majority of people on the Montréal jazz scene have no connection to the Black African American tradition in general,” he believes. “A lot of people who consider themselves the elders of the jazz scene here are too disconnected from the tradition and from its main figures,” says the musician, who hopes for a stronger attachment to this history. It was thanks to a mandatory music class that Modibo discovered music in high school. At CEGEP, he pursued jazz studies in a double program.
Par la suite, il obtient une bourse et q: Afterward, he received a scholarship and left Montréal to study at the University of Toronto. He then returned to his hometown. “In Toronto, I found it harder to integrate diversity into the jazz scene. I decided not to fight that and to come back,” he says. However, he observes that the Montréal scene, while more welcoming, is itself rather homogeneous. “It’s super white, there aren’t a lot of us Black people. The ones who are part of the professional jazz scene, you can count them on your fingers,” he adds.
Tout comme ses collègues Valérie Lacombe: Like his colleagues Valérie Lacombe and Sam Kirmayer, Modibo Keïta lives in Oscar Peterson’s old neighbourhood.
« Il s’agit probablement du pianiste le: “He’s probably the most important pianist after Art Tatum in the history of stride, of jazz. But a lot of people don’t know he’s from Montréal.” He draws a parallel with the career of Kaytranada, a Montréal producer who last year won several Grammys for his latest album. “Kaytranada, who is one of the hottest producers in the world right now, complained that he wasn’t recognized in Quebec, even though he’s a Quebecer. Quebecers feel detached from all of that,” he says, lamenting what he describes as “selective nationalism.”
« Les gens qui suivent sont des Québécoi: “The people who follow are Quebecers from immigrant backgrounds, or anglophones, or people who are immersed in immigrant culture,” he says. Based on his experience, he finds it even harder for a Quebec artist to find an audience. “If you can break through in Quebec as a Black person, you can break through anywhere,” he lets drop, adding that it’s a matter of numbers, since other regions have more potential fans because of their larger populations, but also a matter of social dynamics. It’s well known that musicians aren’t rolling in money, least of all jazz musicians.
« Les gens ne savent pas à quel point c’: “People don’t know how hard it is to be a musician in Montréal, especially a jazz or world music musician,” explains Modibo, citing the cost of living, which has risen dizzyingly since he started out, and musicians’ low pay. In his view, Montréal lacks venues where musicians can perform, and jazz is not promoted enough in the city.
Céline Peterson a le jazz inscrit dans s: Céline Peterson has jazz in her DNA, as she says herself with a laugh from her home in Toronto. “There’s nothing like watching jazz musicians communicate with each other. Nothing is more musically satisfying than being in the audience and watching the musicians have fun, throw creative challenges at each other and trust each other,” says the artist agent and producer.
C’est ce qui fait la beauté du jazz et r: That’s what makes jazz beautiful and makes the shows unique. She is grateful to have been exposed to this style of music, having grown up surrounded by musicians, including her father, Oscar Peterson. “When the musicians are on stage, the whole room vibrates, you can feel it. It’s truly one of the most magical things about this music.” Helping local talent flourish is Céline’s mission, and her passion.
Elle remarque aussi cette nouvelle audie: She has also noticed this new audience, the arrival of young people who want to hear the music, and their excitement is palpable. “Jazz is not one size fits all. There are other genres that people enjoy that come out of jazz. Many young people come to jazz through an artist from another genre who incorporates elements of jazz into their music,” she points out.
Elle note également que certains jeunes: She also notes that some young musicians choose to adopt a style closer to the tradition. “It’s beautiful to see, they’re learning from their elders.”
Céline Peterson, agent and producer. Photo: Courtesy
Si une chose la surprend moins, c’est qu: What surprises her less is how few people know that her father is from here. “It’s important to me to remind people that not only was he a proud Canadian, but that he also never left Canada,” she says of the man who spent the last 30 years of his life in the Greater Toronto Area.
Cependant, ce qui compte à ses yeux, c’e: However, what matters to her is that he is celebrated in the jazz community, as is her aunt, Daisy Sweeney Peterson, who taught piano to her brother Oscar, to Oliver Jones, to Joe Sealey and to so many others. “Jazz and music in Montréal come mainly from Black culture. Tributes and recognition don’t necessarily spread through minority communities in the same way. So I don’t think it’s a problem specific to Montréal or Quebec, I think there are versions of it everywhere.”
Valerie Lacombe et Sam Kirmayer ont fond: Valerie Lacombe and Sam Kirmayer founded the Société jazz de Saint-Henri, an initiative that aims to make jazz a community activity that honours tradition. “We want to offer the community a space to return to this idea: to exchange, to practise an oral tradition, to listen to each other as a community,” explains Valérie Lacombe. Concerts and jazz-related activities are offered in the neighbourhood.
Il n’existe plus que deux clubs de jazz: Only two jazz clubs remain in Montréal: <l1>Upstairs</l1> and <l2>Dièse Onze</l2>. The Société jazz de St-Henri plans to open one soon.
Pour découvrir le jazz, Modibo Keïta sug: To discover jazz, Modibo Keïta suggests the “Jazz Night in America” series on YouTube, which features a variety of concerts by different artists, both well known and lesser known.
